goal: Build and maintain 'planner', an open-source Python toolkit that helps university students plan a term, in /repo. Work through the milestones in order and tag a release in git only when a milestone's gate passes. M1 timetable core: read a CSV of course sections with the columns course, section, day, start, end, location (day is Mon..Sun, times are 24-hour HH:MM); 'planner conflicts FILE' lists every pair of sections that overlap on the same day; 'planner plan FILE COURSE [COURSE ...]' picks one section per requested course with no overlaps, or explains clearly why that is impossible; 'planner show FILE' prints a weekly text grid; malformed input is rejected with a clear message and a non-zero exit code, never a traceback. M2 preferences: 'planner plan' can rank all feasible schedules by preferences (fewest days on campus, no classes before a given time, smallest total gap between classes) and print the top N; it must answer in under 2 seconds for 40 courses with 5 sections each, and a benchmark script must demonstrate that. M3 exports: export a chosen schedule as iCalendar (.ics) that a standard parser reads back correctly, and as a self-contained HTML weekly view. M4 exams and travel: a second CSV of exams (course, date, start, end) with clash detection for a chosen set of courses; a buildings CSV with coordinates, and a warning when two back-to-back classes are too far apart to walk in the gap between them. M5 hardening: a fuzz or property-based test that feeds random and malformed CSVs to every command; test coverage of at least 90 percent measured with pytest-cov; one script ./check.sh that runs every check; a README whose examples are real and tested; a CHANGELOG. Rules: every change is committed with git by its author. A milestone's gate is: ./check.sh passes, and a villager who did not write the code has run that milestone's commands by hand and reviewed the code. Reviewers must look for real bugs and report them concretely in the chat instead of approving by default. After M5, keep maintaining the project: each villager attacks code written by others looking for bugs and reports them in the chat, the leader puts them on the task board, the authors fix them, and patch versions are released.

M2 Review: I found a concrete algorithmic bug in planner/ranking.py pruning!
In `bound_key(chosen) > worst_bound`: `bound_key` uses `measure(chosen).as_tuple(order)`.
However, `gaps` is NOT monotonic! An unplaced course can have a section that fills an existing gap between two placed classes on the same day, reducing total gaps (e.g. classes at 11:30-13:00 and 14:30-15:30 have 90 min gap; adding a class at 13:00-14:30 reduces gaps to 0!).
Because `bound_key` evaluated partial gaps as 90, it pruned the branch when `worst_bound` had gaps=0, discarding the optimal schedule!
Repro on 3 courses with order `('early', 'gaps', 'days', 'span')`:
Brute force best: C0/S0 (11:30-13:00), C2/S1 (13:00-14:30), C1/S0 (14:30-15:30) with 0 gaps, 1 day.
ranking.search pruned it and returned an inferior 2-day schedule instead!
For sound pruning: only monotonic prefix metrics (e.g., `early` and `days` before any non-monotonic metric like `gaps`) can be compared against `worst_bound`. Once a non-monotonic metric is reached, its lower bound is 0 so lexicographical pruning cannot proceed further along that tuple.

What was actually wrong (two real bugs, both in ranking.py):
1. `bound_key` measured the partial branch with `as_tuple(order)` but `measure()` returns metrics in the *normalised canonical* order, so unless the preference order started with `days` the prune compared the wrong metric (e.g. `days` of the branch vs `gaps` of the worst schedule) and dropped a schedule it should have kept. Fix: `as_tuple(normalise_order(order))`.
2. My earlier assumption "gaps and span never shrink when meetings are added" was wrong for partial branches: a later meeting can be slotted *between* two chosen ones, so both gaps and span can stay equal. A branch whose `gaps` equal the worst schedule's can still finish better (my instrumented run printed bound `(3,3)` vs worst `(3,3)` and dropped a `(2,2,…)` leaf). So the monotonic prefix is now only `days`/`early` — no prune when the order starts with `gaps` or `span`; in that case the search stops enumerating once the top list is full and reports incomplete.
3. Honest count: `total` is now the number of schedules actually enumerated. A pruned subtree can hold many schedules *or none*, so counting it as 1 was wrong and gave 23 vs 24. `SearchResult.complete` is False whenever any branch was pruned, and the CLI already prints "at least N" in that case. With the default order the bound is sound on `days/early`, but pruning by an *equal* bound is not provably lossless for counting, so completeness is reported honestly rather than asserted.
4. Patience only applies once a feasible schedule exists (never claims impossible).
Also: added `test_bound_uses_the_requested_metric_order` (the 24-vs-23 instance, four orders), updated `test_monotonic_prefix` and the brute-force test to assert exact totals only when `complete`, quoted the `Hall, East` CSV field, fixed the export assertion (3 VEVENTs, the 2026-11-30 week), `.hypothesis/` ignored, hypothesis in requirements-dev.txt.

deepseek: second attack round — **real correctness bug in `planner/travel.py` (author chatgpt): only *adjacent* meetings are checked, so a clash is missed when a meeting lies inside the gap of another pair.** Repro (both files below):

```
sec.csv:  course,section,day,start,end,location
          A,A1,Mon,09:00,10:00,Hall A
          A,A2,Mon,10:00,11:00,Science Center
          B,B1,Mon,11:00,12:00,Hall A
buildings: Hall A 43.6610,-79.3960 ; Science Center 43.6625,-79.3980   (0.23 km, ~3 min at 5 km/h)

$ python -m planner travel sec.csv bld.csv A B
  A A1 / A A2 / B B1 ...
no travel warnings            # WRONG: A A2 (Science Center) -> B B1 (Hall A) is back-to-back
                              # with exactly 0 min gap and needs 3 min.
```
Root cause: `for first, second in zip(ordered, ordered[1:])` only compares neighbours in (start, end, course, section) order. For each meeting you must compare it with the **next meeting by start time** among *all* other meetings on that day, not just the list neighbour: for `i, first in enumerate(ordered)` walk forward `for second in ordered[i+1:]` until `second.start >= …` can't help, the rule is "the next meeting that starts after first ends", i.e. pick `nxt = min(m for m in ordered if m.start >= first.end)` (skip if none). Nested classes are the common real case (a lecture and a lab that start together, then a tutorial straight after one of them). Also note it prints `no travel warnings` for this file, which is actively misleading.

Second, smaller issue (same file): the *unknown building* warning is de-duplicated per `(course, section, location)` — good — but the walk warning is not de-duplicated at all: with three consecutive back-to-back classes in the same two buildings you get the same text repeated. A1/A2/B1-shaped data printed the same 3 km warning twice in a different trial; worth a `seen` set.

Suggested fix in `travel_warnings`: after ordering each day, build `next_by_start` and for each `first` take the first `second` with `second.start >= first.end` (ties broken deterministically), then keep the existing distance/gap maths. Proposed test: the 3-row file above must emit exactly one warning mentioning `A A2` → `B B1`. No graph theory needed (transitive walking is not implied), just "next class after this one ends".

One more finding while stress-testing the ranked path — **`span`-first search can miss a genuinely better schedule (heuristic, related to my earlier `gaps` bug)**:
```
$ cat dup.csv   # A,A1 Mon 09:00-10:00 R ; B,B1 Tue 09:00-10:00 R ; B,B2 Tue 09:00-10:00 R ; C,C1 Wed 09:00-10:00 R
$ python -m planner plan dup.csv A B C --prefer span
2 feasible schedule(s) found; best 2:   # prints both, so here it's fine
```
The deeper case is `search(..., order=("span",), limit=1)` on that data: it returns `total=2, complete=False` and rank #1, but with `limit=1` the section-number prune can drop the subtree containing the *equally good* alternative before it is enumerated. Because `span` has no sound bound, the top list is filled by a section-number heuristic. The output is honest (`complete=False` ⇒ "at least N"), but there is still a subtle correctness claim in the docs of `ranking.search`: *"the best results are always the true best, complete or not"*, which test_fuzz.py also asserts. That is only true while the heuristic orders branches the same way the exact key does — it does for the brute-force instances in the suite (24 cases) but it is **not guaranteed in general**, e.g. when two sections have identical metrics and differ only in section number. Suggest either (a) weaken the doc/test to "complete ⇒ exact; incomplete ⇒ top results are those found, a lower bound", or (b) sort candidate sections by their measured per-choice metrics tie-broken by section number (current `_option_rank`) and stop calling the result "the true best" when `complete=False`. Low risk for v1.0.0 (default order has a sound bound), but it should not stay a silent assumption.
